> 
> ## 4. Fastest documented revenue motion
> 
> **Corey Ganim's model is the fastest with real numbers attached**: a $999, same-week diagnostic call, no product built, no audience required, 40% convert to $3–10K implementation. He states the offer works "with zero audience and zero capital." [Source](https://x.com/gregisenberg/status/2077471201002185195), [Source](https://x.com/coreyganim/status/2041983671855649034)
> 
> Second-fastest, less rigorously documented: **cold-outreach automation gigs** — one secondary source claims "5 clients, $6,400 in 28 days" for a done-for-you AI outreach service, and general guidance across several of these sources converges on the same advice: **your first paying client comes from someone who already trusts you (a warm relationship), not cold outreach, and the first engagement should be priced low or free in exchange for a case study** — one source specifies $50–150 for the pilot. [Source](https://money-lab.app/blog/how-to-get-first-ai-automation-client-2026) This is **unverified pattern advice**, not a documented individual outcome, and should be weighted lower than the Ganim numbers.
> 
> **Contrast for calibration**: Wyndo took **6 months at $0** before any revenue appeared, and this was a newsletter/audience-first path, not a services path. Audience-first is the slow motion; diagnostic-call-first is the fast one.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## 5. Domain experts in regulated industries — the closest analog (most important finding)
> 
> This is where the research came up genuinely thin, and that thinness is itself a finding worth reporting plainly: **searching specifically for named individual domain experts in pharma, healthcare, finance, or legal who personally built and sold an AI product, with disclosed revenue, turned up almost nothing at the individual-practitioner level.** What exists instead:
> 
> - **Kevin Steele (finance-adjacent, the strongest individual match found).** Fractional CFO, no prior coding background, built a working FP&amp;A application in Claude Code in ~6 weeks, now serving paying clients, running at $160/month in tooling cost against a claimed $8,000/year saving versus the software it replaced. [Source](https://www.cfoconnect.eu/resources/event-recaps/claude-code-finance-app-fpa-build/) This is the single clearest "domain expert, regulated-adjacent field, built and monetized" case found. It is one data point, not a pattern.
> - **CPA firm advisory upsell (finance, regulated, but the tool wasn't built by the domain expert — it was bought).** A 12-person Phoenix CPA firm doing $1.2M revenue at 15% margin used an AI vendor (Uncle Kam) to free 35 hours/month of senior CPA time, launched a new advisory line, and closed 23 engagements at an $8,500 average fee — $195,500 in incremental advisory revenue in year one. [Source](https://unclekam.com/tax-strategy-blog/2026-accounting-software-ai-driven-tools-tax-pros-need/) This is the **strongest documented pattern for "AI capability turns domain expertise into new billable advisory revenue"** — but the practitioners here are buyers of AI, not builders.
> - **Graph AI (pharma safety/regulatory, but technical founders importing domain expertise, not the reverse).** Four founders with zero pharmacology background built an AI-native pharmacovigilance platform, hired a doctor to embed domain knowledge, and spent 4 months on FDA computer-system validation, SOC 2, and CFR 21 Part 11 compliance before it was sellable. Result: adverse-event processing cut from 3+ hours to 10 minutes, 65% cost savings, 300+ drugs monitored for enterprise customers. [Source](https://www.bvp.com/atlas/graph-ai-a-service-firm-turned-ai-native-solution-for-pharma-and-life-sciences) This is the inverse of what was asked for, but it is the most concrete evidence in the whole research set of **what it actually costs to sell software into a regulated pharma workflow** — months of compliance work, an advisor network, and eventually a technical team. It is not a solo non-technical builder's path; it's the ceiling above it.
> - **Essay-level claims with no named cases.** Two independently written essays (Built In, and an unaffiliated blog by Aaron Brethorst) both argue forcefully that domain experts in regulated fields (healthcare operations, clinical coding, payroll/actuarial, logistics compliance) are AI's biggest winners — and **neither cites a single named individual with disclosed revenue**. Built In's own examples are explicitly hypothetical ("a healthcare operations director with 15 years in prior-authorization workflows...") or an internal reference to the author's own company. [Source](https://builtin.com/articles/ai-rewards-domain-knowledge)
> 
> **Bottom line on Q5**: the "domain expert in a regulated industry monetizes AI capability" story is widely asserted and thinly documented at the individual level. The closest real analogs found are (a) a solo finance professional (Kevin Steele) building his own tool to serve existing clients, and (b) domain expertise being imported into an AI-native venture from outside (Graph AI), rather than an insider building it themselves. This gap is a genuine finding, not a search failure — it suggests the pharma/healthcare/legal/finance "solo builder monetizes deep expertise + AI" case study largely doesn't exist yet in public, searchable form, or is happening privately (advisory retainers, not-for-attribution consulting) rather than as a public content-marketed story the way ecommerce and marketing pivots are.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## 6. What fails — genuinely critical findings
> 
> - **Security is the recurring, embarrassing failure mode**, and it hits non-technical builders specifically because they lack the judgment to catch it. Moltbook (AI social network, founder publicly said he "didn't write a single line of code") had its production database — 1.5M API tokens, 35,000 emails — fully exposed 3 days after launch. Quittr hit $1M revenue in 10 days, then its Firebase database was found publicly readable, exposing 39,000+ users. [Sources](https://tech.yahoo.com/cybersecurity/articles/another-top-vibe-coding-platform-160300340.html), techradar coverage of the same events.
> - **Public mockery when it goes wrong, from technical people specifically.** One vibe coder posted "Guys, I'm under attack" after users found their SaaS's API keys unprotected, then admitted "I'm not technical so this is taking me longer than usual to figure out." A computer scientist responded publicly: **"Quick reminder: I'm charging $1,000/hour to fix your vibe-coded mess."** [Source](https://pivot-to-ai.com/2025/03/18/guys-im-under-attack-ai-vibe-coding-in-the-wild/) This is the sharpest documented instance of non-technical credibility collapsing in public.
> - **The "vibe coding is a scam" backlash is real and dated** — multiple pieces (Medium, HN, a Substack titled "Remember Vibe Coders? Yeah… They're Gone") argue the initial hype cycle already curdled, calling it a "dangerous fantasy" that technical knowledge is optional. [Source](https://nmn.gl/blog/vibe-coding-fantasy)
> - **AI consultants without real technical depth get quietly filtered out, not called out.** No high-profile individual takedown of a specific non-technical AI consultant was found (searched directly for this). What exists instead is structural criticism: McKinsey's own 2025 State of AI survey found 60% of organizations get little to no measurable AI value — attributed to a shortage of people who can actually deploy it, which cuts against any consultant selling surface-level advice. [Source](https://www.tredence.com/blog/ai-consultant-skills)
> - **Selling into a genuinely regulated pipeline (not just "regulated-adjacent" like a CPA advisory upsell) is not a solo, fast, non-technical motion.** Graph AI needed 4 months of FDA/SOC2/CFR21 work with a funded team even after they had domain expertise on staff. That is the honest ceiling on what a lone builder — technical or not — can promise a pharma company for anything touching adverse events, submissions, or patient data.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## 7. What a non-technical builder can do that a technical one structurally cannot
> 
> - **Verify correctness in the domain, not just correctness of the code.** Brethorst's essay states this precisely: an AI can generate code that "compiles, passes tests... and is subtly, expensively incorrect" in domain terms — and only someone who has actually reconciled a thousand payrolls, or sat through a thousand HCP objections, catches that. The engineer cannot verify what they don't know to check. [Source](https://www.brethorsting.com/blog/2026/05/domain-expertise-has-always-been-the-real-moat/)
> - **Sell the diagnosis before the build exists, and be trusted doing it.** Corey Ganim's whole model works because a small business owner will let a fellow operator sit with their calendar and workflows in a way they wouldn't let an unknown developer — the sale is trust-in-judgment, not trust-in-code.
> - **Speak the buyer's language natively, in a regulated field where jargon-fluency is itself a gate.** In pharma, "market access," "prior authorization," "HCP engagement," "MSL" are not learnable from a prompt in a way that reads as credible to the buyer — they are proof of having sat in the room. This is asserted repeatedly across sources but, per Q5, rarely evidenced with a named case.
> - **What this is not**: it is not evidence that non-technical builders write better code, ship faster, or avoid security failures — the opposite is documented (Q6). The advantage is specifically in judgment about what "right" means inside the domain, and in the trust a domain peer extends that an outside engineer doesn't get by default.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Survivorship bias — explicit flag
> 
> Every named figure in this research is a survivor by construction — they were findable because they succeeded enough to be written about. Wyndo states plainly that he made $0 for 6 months; that's the closest thing to a documented "it didn't work at first" data point in the whole set. No source surfaced a comparable non-technical builder who tried this and failed publicly and stayed visible — failures in this space appear to go quiet rather than get written up, which is itself worth noting: the absence of failure stories is not absence of failure, it's a reporting bias in a survivorship-biased genre.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## The two to three models that transfer to a pharma domain expert with no audience
> 
> 1. **The diagnostic-call-to-implementation model (Corey Ganim).** Sell a paid assessment of where a pharma commercial, market-access, or customer-intelligence function is losing time or leaving signal on the table — priced high enough to filter ($999–2,000), delivered same week, with an implementation upsell. No audience needed; needs only a handful of warm relationships from a pharma commercial career. This is the fastest-cash model documented and the one with the most concrete numbers behind it.
> 
> 2. **The build-for-your-own-practice-first model (Kevin Steele).** Build the tool in Claude Code to serve one's own existing consulting relationships — not as a SaaS product sold cold, but as a working artifact that becomes the proof and the delivery mechanism at once. This avoids the regulatory-compliance cliff entirely (Graph AI's 4-month CSV/SOC2/CFR21 grind) because the tool never leaves a trusted advisory relationship to become independently-sold software.
> 
> 3. **The AI-accelerated advisory upsell inside an existing regulated practice (the CPA-firm pattern, adapted).** Rather than building or selling AI tools at all, use AI capability to do existing commercial-intelligence or customer-strategy consulting work faster and deeper, and sell the freed-up capacity as a new premium service line to existing pharma relationships — the $195,500 CPA advisory result is the clearest documented proof this specific move works, even though in that case the domain expert was a buyer of AI rather than a builder.
> 
> **What does not transfer**: the venture-scale "build software that actually enters a pharma regulatory or safety workflow" path (Graph AI). That requires a funded team, months of compliance work, and importing rather than possessing the domain expertise — it is the wrong template for a solo builder starting from zero audience.

The non-technical research came back, and the most interesting result is what wasn't found.

## Your exact profile doesn't exist publicly

- Searching for named domain experts in pharma, healthcare, finance or legal who built and sold AI capability turned up **almost nothing at the individual level.**
- The claim that domain experts are AI's big winners is **everywhere in essays and nowhere in named cases with real numbers.**
- **Two readings, and both are true:** the position is unclaimed, and nobody has proven it pays.
- The honest one in the middle: this work is probably happening privately as advisory retainers, not as public content.

## The one close analog

- **A fractional CFO, not technical, built his own finance tool in Claude Code in six weeks.** He doesn't sell the tool. He uses it to serve his existing clients.
- **The tool is the credential, not the product.** That's the pattern that fits you.
- The reverse case is instructive too: an AI pharma startup with four technical founders **had to hire a doctor** and spend four months on FDA compliance. **They had to buy what you already have.**

## The fastest documented money in the whole search

- **A non-technical operator charges $999 for a 45-minute diagnostic call.** Delivered same week, no product, no audience.
- **40% of those buy implementation at $3,000 to $10,000.**
- His own words on why he wins: **"They don't need a developer and they definitely don't need another course. What they need is someone who looks at their calendar, inbox, and workflows and says: this tool, this process, this is where you start."**
- Swap his small-business buyer for your pharma data leader and that's your offer.

## The line that answers your question directly

- From an essay on this exact problem: **"You cannot prompt your way to domain expertise. The binding constraint in software has shifted from building systems to knowing whether those systems produce right answers."**
- **You can tell whether the answer is right. That's the scarce part**, and it's the thing you've done for a decade.

## The failure mode to respect

- **Non-technical builders get burned publicly on security.** One shipped an app with an open database exposing 39,000 users. Another posted "I'm under attack" and a professional replied he charges $1,000 an hour to clean up vibe-coded messes.
- **In pharma this is fatal, not embarrassing.** Anything touching patient data or adverse events needs compliance work you can't shortcut.
- **So sell judgment and build for your own practice. Don't sell software into a regulated pipeline.**

## What I'd actually do with this

- **A paid diagnostic, priced to filter, delivered in a week, sold to people who already know you.** Documented, fast, needs no audience.
- **Your builds serve your delivery, not the market.** They're proof you're current, and they make the diagnostic faster.
- **Skip anything that needs an audience to work.** That's a year away.

**One next action:** the model above runs entirely on warm relationships, which makes the names the actual bottleneck now. Who from the Medikly, Cambridge, Ashfield or SG years picks up the phone?

Catalant (2–5 day approval, 20–30% take) and Torc (self-reported 7.6-day average placement, unverified) are the next-fastest. Malt has the most transparent freelancer-favorable take rate (10% then 5%) but is Europe-weighted. Toptal, Braintrust, A.Team, BTG are all multi-week-to-months before producing income — apply in parallel, don't plan around them. Clutch/GoodFirms/LinkedIn Services all require reviews or an audience you don't have yet; they compound after the first few engagements, not before.

> GLG, Dialectica, Coleman/VisasQ, and Prosapient are truly open self-serve applications with no portfolio or audience required — a real structural fit for zero-audience credentials. Realistic first cash is 3–6 weeks out, and first month's income is modest ($200–500), not primary revenue. - **A two-week AI readiness sprint sells for €2,300 to €4,200.** Named firm, live page.

- **The fastest path runs on relationships that already exist.** That's not my opinion anymore, it's what the research found.

Here's the ICP in one read.

## Who actually buys

- **Three roles, not one "data leader."**
- **The economic buyer** is board-accountable, controls budget and vendor payment, and keeps re-raising the same unresolved architecture problem across years without it getting fixed.
- **A product owner** sits under him, fighting for budget and resources.
- **The people who feel the pain daily are usually not the ones who sign.** Write for them, sell to the first one.
- **A second, smaller buyer exists:** a non-technical mission lead with a data-dependent idea and no budget yet, who needs a right-sized approach to take back to her group.

## The strongest finding in the whole corpus

- **A shadow system the client built because they stopped trusting the one that was designed for them.** They gave it their own name.
- Confirmed independently in **four separate files across different engagements**, months apart.
- One of them, on why: **"they didn't trust the manipulation from core... they were looking at the output and they were like, something's going on, they don't trust it, they pull their own version."**
- The buyer's own retrospective: **"The fact that the unified layer was messed up, duplication and a bunch of stuff... why didn't we address that then?"**

## What hurts, in their words

- **"I don't know," from the people who are supposed to be the source of truth.** Thirty-plus instances, disproportionately senior.
- **"We're kind of flying blind."** Said about a vendor nobody could oversee.
- **"Black box."** Used independently by different people in different meetings for the same core system.
- **"I can't drive in the dark here."** A program manager who can't report status because nobody can tell him what data sources exist.
- **Duplicates with no naming convention.** At one point two versions of the core data, 800 tables each.
- **Undocumented scripts loading production tables**, no source control, no logging, nobody able to say how often they ran or what they changed.

## What they asked to buy

- **A scoped assessment priced as an option, not a commitment.** Go look, tell us what's there, then price the fix.
- **Someone to oversee a vendor they couldn't manage themselves.**
- **A named owner for governance and access**, asked for out loud, aimed at the budget holder.
- That first one is a buyer agreeing to pay to find out the size of the problem. **That's the offer.**

## The job to be done

> When my team has quietly built undocumented workarounds because they don't trust the system we designed, I want an outside, scoped assessment of what actually exists, so I can make a real decision instead of guessing.

## What the job postings add

- **Same failure from the outside:** 75.5% of postings mention AI, only 15% say which decision it serves.
- **Your own conclusion:** organizations don't fail at AI because they hire the wrong people, they fail because they skip operating model design.
- Hiring happens at director level (23.9%) far more than C-suite (2.9%), so the operating model never gets designed where it could be.
- **One seat, four jobs** is the standard posting: strategist, salesperson, manager, thought leader.

**The line that connects everything:** they cannot see what they actually have, and they are spending money as if they can.

> When an agency needs to operationalize AI across functions under compliance and delivery pressure, I want to stand up an AI operating system that automates workflows and drives measurable adoption, so I can reduce cycle time and create differentiation.

That one is yours already, written off a real posting with each clause cited.

- **Deadline risk:** the platform can't do the real client work and someone can feel a delivery date slipping.
- **Locked out:** people blocked from raw data and documentation they need.
- **Can't report status:** a program manager who can't say where things stand because nobody can list the data sources.

Honest answer: lanes yes, skeptic no. That's a gap I should own — several of today's research runs went straight from lanes to my own merge, with no adversarial pass.

## Where this run stands against the diamond

- **Planner: done**, inline rather than as a recorded step.
- **Lanes: three, running blind**, none told your prior conclusions.
- **Skeptic: not yet.** There's nothing to attack until the lanes return, but it was also missing from today's earlier runs.
- **Merge: mine.** Which is exactly why the skeptic matters, since the merger shouldn't be the only check.

## What the skeptic will attack

- **Sample honesty.** How many postings were actually retrieved in full versus glimpsed in a search snippet, and whether the counts have a real denominator.
- **Survivorship in the search.** Job boards surface what's indexable. Small companies posting only on their own site get missed, which would bias the sample toward big names.
- **Whether the patterns are real or read into the data.** Any claim without a quote gets cut.
- **Whether the findings just agree with your 2025 thesis.** If the fresh scan happens to confirm everything you already believed, that's suspicious, not reassuring.

## On your small-to-mid hypothesis

- **Probably right, and for a specific reason: procurement.** Big pharma runs vendor onboarding, master agreements and security review. Six to twelve months before a first invoice.
- A mid-size biotech can sign in weeks because one executive owns the decision.
- **The refinement I'd make: commercial-stage is the real filter, not size.** A company with one to three launched products has real customer data problems, actual revenue, and no large internal data team.
- **Pre-commercial biotech is the trap.** They look small and fast, but they have no commercial data yet, so there's nothing for you to assess.
- Both lanes now tag every posting by size bracket so we can test this rather than assume it.

**One next action:** when the lanes land I'll run the skeptic before showing you anything, and the merge will say what survived and what got killed.

**Claude** · `5cbe7051-0cc3-4374-a66e-6257d2a52fce`

The fractional and contract lane came back, and it's mostly a null result — which is itself the finding.

## The number that matters

- **Six live paid engagements found across roughly 40 platforms and firms. None at your level.**
- **Zero of the six are assessments or audits.** All six are twelve-month delivery builds.
- Rates on what's live: $25 to $60 an hour for data analyst contracts, $100 to $120 for change management.

## Why the null result isn't bad news

- **Nobody posts a job req for a two-week consulting assessment.** That work is sold, not posted.
- So job boards measure employment demand, not consulting demand. **We were looking in the wrong place for your offer.**
- The absence tells you where the offer doesn't come from. It says nothing about whether it sells.

## Fractional platforms are dead for this niche

- **Zero live healthcare or life-sciences openings across nine named platforms.**
- Continuum, Bolster, Toptal, Upwork are bench-and-match models, not job boards. "Graphite" as a fractional marketplace doesn't appear to exist.
- **One real board does exist: fractionaljobs.io.** Currently empty in your niche, but its closed listings show the rate: **$175 to $225 an hour** for fractional data leads and CTOs.
- Go Fractional publishes a benchmark of **$208 an hour average for fractional chief data officers.**

## Expert networks can't be searched, only joined

- **None of the six publish what they're seeking.** Demand is generated behind a login and by cold outreach.
- The only way in is to register and wait. That's an afternoon, not a search.
- Rate estimates in the $250 to $800 per call range are anecdotal, not confirmed.

## Your size instinct held up

- **Every real fractional listing found was at a small or startup healthcare company**, not large pharma.
- Boutique consultancy benches are mostly dead: ten of fifteen firms show full-time hiring only. Two exceptions run standing contractor programs.
- One is explicit that it wants fifteen to twenty-five years of experience and says plainly: **"We do not offer one-hour consults."**

## What I'd do with this

- **Register with the expert networks this week.** No search needed, no audience needed, and it's the only channel where your credentials alone open the door.
- **Create profiles on fractionaljobs.io and Go Fractional now**, so you're vetted before a listing appears rather than applying cold after.
- **Stop treating job boards as a source of consulting work.** They're useful for reading the market, not for finding your buyer.

The two job-posting lanes are still running. Skeptic goes after all three before I merge anything.

> ## 3. Analysis
> 
> **1. What problem is each posting trying to solve? (quoted)**
> - **IQVIA:** consolidating identity across data sources — "Own the strategy, roadmap, and operational management of IQVIA Digital's Identity Graph capabilities."
> - **Real Chemistry:** operationalizing generative AI — "This position is crucial in driving the execution of AI strategies at Real Chemistry, ensuring that AI initiatives are practical, effective, and aligned with real-world needs."
> - **Precision AQ:** consolidating fragmented legacy data — "We are building the Data Hub, a centralized data platform responsible for consolidating legacy data infrastructure."
> - **Tiger Analytics:** standing up a data product from nothing for a specific drug launch — "own the end-to-end commercial data product for a kidney launch, from vision to execution... ability to operate independently in greenfield / build-from-scratch environments."
> - **Doceree:** none of this is retrofitted onto legacy systems — "every layer of their stack is being built in-house, in production."
> 
> **2. How many postings ask one person to cover strategy + delivery + people management + BD/revenue, all in one seat?**
> Reading only the full-text postings, **2 of 39 combine all four explicitly in quoted language**: Inizio's Data and AI Strategy Lead ("strategizing, designing, and delivering enterprise-grade Data and AI solutions" + "lead a growing matrixed Data Science and AI Team" + "driving revenue and sales targets by identifying and pursuing new opportunities") and Real Chemistry's Managing Director, Insights and Analytics ("Own and grow a $3M+ portfolio" + "Mentor and in some cases directly manage Directors, Senior Managers, and Analysts" + "Oversee the strategic design"). A further **4 combine three of the four** (CMI's Director and VP, Digital Marketing Analytics roles; Real Chemistry's Senior Director, Advertising Analytics; Tiger Analytics' Commercial Data Product role) — all missing an explicit BD/revenue line, present on the other three axes.
> 
> **3. How many mention managing/coordinating other agencies, vendors, or partners?**
> **3 of 39, explicitly.** IQVIA's Product Lead, HCP &amp; Consumer Graph ("Manage strategic vendor and data partner relationships that support identity resolution, graph enrichment, signal acquisition"); IQVIA's Product Manager, Audience Platforms — Integrations ("Monitors integration health and success metrics... partner adoption," naming LiveRamp, Experian, DSPs, SSPs by name); and Inizio's Data and AI Strategy Lead, which is coordination across sibling agencies inside the same holding company ("collaboration with the Inizio wide Advisory businesses and leaders") rather than external vendors — a different, internal-network version of the same pattern.
> 
> **4. Seniority distribution (of the 39 read in full):**
> Director-and-above (Director/Assoc. Director/Sr. Director/VP/Managing Director/Principal): **18 (46%)**. Manager-level: **~9 (23%)**. Individual-contributor/senior IC (Analyst, Consultant, Engineer, Data Scientist): **~10 (26%)**. Entry/trainee: **2 (5%)**. This sample skews senior — a real, if partial, artifact of which postings surface well in search and which career pages I could actually fetch.
> 
> **5. Concrete decision/metric/workflow named vs. general transformation language:**
> **24 of 39 name something concrete** — a specific dataset (claims, EMR, DRG, IQVIA Xponent), a specific metric (match rates, delivery success, latency), or a specific workflow (measurement and analysis plans, campaign blueprint development). **15 lean on general language** ("drive AI initiatives," "champion data integrity," "evolve engagement models") without naming the underlying mechanism.
> 
> **6. Named vendors/platforms, with counts across full-text postings:**
> IQVIA (named by 4 different orgs as a data source, not just as itself) · Snowflake (4) · Python/SQL (7, treated as one pairing) · Power BI (4) · Tableau (3) · AWS (4) · Komodo (as a competitor data source, 2) · Salesforce (2) · OpenAI/Anthropic/Claude (3, all Real Chemistry and Doceree AI roles) · LiveRamp, Experian (1 each, IQVIA) · DRG, McKesson, Symphony (1 each, Precision AQ) · Quid, BrandWatch, Meltwater (Real Chemistry insights stack).
> 
> **7. Compensation ranges where shown (18 of 39 disclosed a range):**
> Widest spread: IQVIA Insights and Analytics Principal, $137,200–$453,700. Highest floor: Real Chemistry Managing Director, $215,000. Narrowest/most junior: Veeva ADP entry program, $82,500 flat. CMI Media Group is the most transparent single organization — all 5 of its full-read postings carry a disclosed range.
> 
> **8. Agencies vs. consultancies vs. data vendors — do they ask for different things?**
> Yes, clearly, in the full-text set. **Agencies** (Real Chemistry, CMI, Klick) ask for client-facing storytelling layered on top of the analytics — "Bridge the gap between technical data...and business-critical storytelling," "Derive insights and create PowerPoint stories." **Data vendors** (IQVIA, Veeva, Komodo) ask for platform/product ownership with named integration partners and hard reliability metrics — "match rates, delivery success, latency, partner adoption." **Consultancies** (Tiger Analytics, Inizio) ask for the most compressed skill stack — strategy, delivery, and revenue generation in the same person, and explicitly want people comfortable in "greenfield / build-from-scratch environments" rather than maintaining an existing system.
> 
> **9. What surprised me:**
> The IPG Health / Omnicom Health merger (completed November 2025) means two names on the original organization list are now one entity — a structural fact the original brief couldn't have anticipated. Second: McCann Health has zero open postings of any kind, not just zero in scope — the agency isn't hiring for anything right now. Third: aggregator staleness was worse than expected — multiple postings found via BuiltIn/ZipRecruiter/search snippets were confirmed closed on direct check (one explicitly "removed June 29, 2026," another "removed January 12, 2026"), meaning snippet-only counts from any of these boards should not be trusted as current without a direct open.

**Claude** · `0a665c2c-2ec1-45b4-9e42-3dd0bc614e56`

The agency lane is back, and your vocabulary method produced the single most useful finding of the day.

## The market doesn't say "customer data"

- **The phrase almost never appears in these postings.** What they actually say is **"claims data," "claims and EMR data," "real-world data," "real-world evidence."**
- **"Decision Science" is a title.** So is **"AI Business Partner."** One firm calls its team **"Integrated Intelligence."**
- **"Data product" is real and specific:** one posting is to "own the end-to-end commercial data product for a kidney launch."
- Searching on the real vocabulary surfaced roles my original terms would have missed entirely.
- **This is a positioning problem for you.** You've been calling it customer data strategy. Your buyers call it something else.

## What they pay

- **IQVIA insights principal: $137,200 to $453,700.** Ten-plus years required.
- **Real Chemistry managing director: $215,000 to $225,000**, owning a $3M portfolio.
- Director-level analytics at agencies runs $130,000 to $180,000.
- **Nearly half the postings read were director level or above.**

## What they actually want done

- **Consolidating fragmented legacy data.** One firm is literally "building the Data Hub, a centralized data platform responsible for consolidating legacy data infrastructure."
- **Owning identity across sources.** Another owns "the strategy, roadmap, and operational management of the Identity Graph."
- **Making AI practical.** One posting exists to ensure "AI initiatives are practical, effective, and aligned with real-world needs."
- **Greenfield work.** Consultancies explicitly want people comfortable "in greenfield, build-from-scratch environments."

## The three buyer types want different things

- **Agencies** want analytics plus storytelling: "bridge the gap between technical data and business-critical storytelling."
- **Data vendors** want platform ownership with hard numbers: match rates, latency, partner adoption.
- **Consultancies** want the most compressed stack, and they're the ones asking one person to do strategy, delivery, management and revenue.

## Honest limits on this lane

- **39 postings read in full out of about 75 surfaced.** The rest were search snippets, and several turned out to be already closed.
- **Boutique firms were never researched.** That batch got cut when I told the agent to stop waiting. That's a real gap, not a finding of zero.
- Several sites blocked access entirely, which is not the same as having no openings.

## What this changes

- **Your language needs to match theirs before anything else gets written.** Site, outreach, offer.
- **The claim that everyone asks one person to do four jobs is weaker than expected:** only 2 of 39 did it explicitly. That thesis needs softening.
- **Two thirds name something concrete**, so the market is less vague than your 2025 analysis suggested.

**One next action:** the pharma lane is still running. When it lands I'll run the skeptic against all three, then bring you what survived, including whether the boutique gap needs a second pass.

---

> ## The four analysis questions that need exact quotes
> 
> ### 1. What problem are these postings actually trying to solve?
> 
> **Fragmented data, no single view.** Novartis (Toronto): *"Own and evolve a single, trusted view of business‑critical data across Commercial, Medical Affairs, and Value &amp; Access."* Sun Pharma: *"Lead the company-wide initiative to identify, consolidate, and harmonize commercial, operational, and market-related data."*
> 
> **AI adoption that hasn't scaled yet.** J&amp;J: *"build and scale enterprise-grade AI capabilities."* Takeda: *"transform the organization by harnessing the power of data, analytics, artificial intelligence, agentic and intelligent automation."* Novartis: *"Champion the exploration and integration of cutting-edge AI technologies."*
> 
> **Commercial data is expensive and nobody owns buying it well.** AbbVie's Category Management posting exists because licensing IQVIA, Symphony, TriNetX, Flatiron, Optum, and Komodo separately is apparently enough of a mess that a dedicated sourcing/contracting director is the fix, not a data architect.
> 
> **Personalized channel decisioning ("Next Best Engagement/Action") is being built, not finished.** Novo Nordisk's Data Scientist II owns *"end-to-end delivery of Next Best Engagement (NBE) data science work-streams"* including *"causal measurement frameworks (test vs. control, A/B testing, holdouts, quasi-experiments)"* — language that describes infrastructure being stood up now, not maintained.
> 
> ### 2. What capability is missing, judged by what one person is asked to do?
> 
> Sun Pharma's Senior Director owns forecasting models, market research vendor management, dashboards/KPIs, team-building, *and* business development support in one seat: *"Serve as key contributor to business development evaluations and strategic partnerships."* Four sub-functions in one hire suggests the commercial-analytics function at that company is being stood up from nothing, not expanded.
> 
> Jazz says this out loud, which is unusual: one of its postings states the company is *"adopting a new product-oriented operating model to enable cross-functional teams to build global capabilities."* Read plainly: analytics work used to be scattered, ad hoc requests with no single owner, and the fix is naming a person as the owner of each capability.
> 
> AbbVie's procurement-titled role is also asked to make an analytics judgment call — *"Identify opportunities to improve data quality"* — inside a sourcing job. That suggests no analytics function currently owns data quality end-to-end; it's been handed to whoever buys the data.
> 
> ### 3. Seniority distribution (n=33, the full-text-confirmed-live set)
> 
> | Level | Count | Share |
> |---|---|---|
> | VP / Executive Director / Head | 4 | 12% |
> | Senior Director | 5 | 15% |
> | Director | 5 | 15% |
> | Associate Director | 12 | 36% |
> | Senior Manager / Manager | 4 | 12% |
> | Individual contributor (senior) | 3 | 9% |
> | C-suite (CDO, Chief AI Officer, etc.) | 0 | 0% |
> 
> Associate Director is the dominant level by a wide margin. **Zero of the 33 confirmed-live postings are C-suite.** (One agent found that Royalty Pharma *appointed* a Head of AI in April 2026 — that's a completed hire mentioned in news coverage, not an open posting, so it's not counted here.)
> 
> ### 4. How many stack strategy + delivery + people management + business development into one seat?
> 
> Judged against the ~20 postings with rich enough text to score this: **one stacks all four cleanly** — Sun Pharma's Senior Director (strategy: *"lead the development and execution of advanced analytics strategies"*; delivery: owns forecasting models directly; people: *"build and mentor a high-performing team"*; BD: the business-development quote above). Roughly six more stack three of the four, almost always missing the explicit BD piece — J&amp;J's VP, Jazz's Suite Lead, Regeneron's Hyderabad Director, and AbbVie's Category Management AD (whose contract-negotiation language is BD-adjacent but framed as procurement, not new-business BD) all fall here.
> 
> ### 5. Outcome specificity: concrete metric/workflow vs. general "transformation" language
> 
> Of the ~20 judged: roughly **12 name a concrete decision, metric, or workflow** — Novo Nordisk's causal A/B testing framework, Amgen's named data sources (*"hcp and account-level demand data, claims data, electronic medical records data, specialty pharmacy data"*), Jazz's KPI frameworks and marketing mix modeling, AbbVie's RFP/RFQ/MSA/SOW procurement metrics. Roughly **8 lean on general transformation language** — Takeda's *"harnessing the power of data,"* J&amp;J's *"AI-first organization,"* Novartis's *"AI culture champion."* This is a real split, not a landslide either way.
> 
> ### 6. Named vendors and platforms, with counts (across all full-text postings, live and closed, n≈40)
> 
> | Vendor/platform | Approx. mentions |
> |---|---|
> | Tableau | 8 |
> | IQVIA (incl. named sub-products) | 8 |
> | Power BI | 6 |
> | Veeva (CRM/Vault) | 6 |
> | AWS | 6 |
> | Snowflake | 5 |
> | Azure | 5 |
> | Symphony Health | 4 |
> | Databricks | 4 |
> | Python / R / SQL (generic stack) | 8+ |
> 
> Only one posting (Novartis) named a specific generative-AI model vendor (GPT, BERT, Cohere) — most "AI" postings describe AI in strategy language without naming which AI platform they mean.
> 
> ### 7. Salary ranges
> 
> **26 of the 33 fully-confirmed-live postings (79%) disclosed a specific salary range.** The 7 that didn't were mostly non-US roles (India GCC positions at Regeneron and Takeda, Toronto) plus two US roles — AbbVie's North Chicago Director role notably did not disclose despite Illinois having a pay-transparency law, which is worth a second look if it matters to you.
> 
> ### 8. What surprised me
> 
> - **A procurement/category-management title showing up as a "commercial data" job.** AbbVie is hiring a contract negotiator, not a data scientist, to fix its data-sourcing mess.
> - **India Global Capability Centers as the actual site of new senior data/AI leadership hiring** — not just execution offshoring. This showed up independently at Regeneron (*"a foundational member of Regeneron's first GCC"*), Takeda (its new Bengaluru "Innovation Capability Center"), and Novartis (a director whose job is explicitly to liaise with the India team). Three companies, same pattern, unprompted.
> - **A third of everything I opened in full was already dead** — filled, expired, or removed — despite still being indexed and served up by search engines and job boards as current.
> - **Two of the ~30 small/mid biotechs on the expanded list had been acquired since being added to anyone's list of independent companies**: Blueprint Medicines (bought by Sanofi, mid-2025) and Apellis (bought by Biogen, May 2026). Blueprint's own careers page shows zero data/analytics openings now — the seat disappears the moment the acquisition closes.
> - **Several small biotechs show a confirmed, high-confidence zero** — not "we couldn't find it," but a direct read of their own career page showing no such role exists: Rhythm Pharmaceuticals, Krystal Biotech, and (with slightly less confidence) Ultragenyx.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Split by size, type, and brand — the comparison you asked for
> 
> **By company size** (bracket is Inferred from employee counts found during research or general market knowledge, not always stated in the postings themselves):
> 
> | Bracket | Companies with a confirmed-live posting | Full-live postings found |
> |---|---|---|
> | Large-cap (~15,000+ employees) | J&amp;J, AbbVie, Novartis, Novo Nordisk, Amgen, Takeda, Sun Pharma, CSL Behring, Daiichi Sankyo | 15 |
> | Mid-cap (~2,000–15,000) | Regeneron, Vertex, Moderna, BioNTech, Alnylam | 9 |
> | Small-cap (&lt;2,000) | Jazz Pharmaceuticals, Pharmacosmos | 8 (7 of those 8 are Jazz alone) |
> 
> The most interesting thing here isn't the bracket totals — it's the **variance inside "small-cap."** Jazz (~2,400 employees) produced more fully-verified live postings than any single large-cap company, and the most internally-structured naming convention of anyone in the whole study (Suite Leads, Global Capability Owners). Meanwhile Ionis, Sarepta, Ultragenyx, Rhythm, Krystal Biotech, and Madrigal — all in the same rough size class — show zero-to-one confirmed live postings, several a confirmed zero. Small doesn't predict "no seat." It predicts "all or nothing": either a company like Jazz has decided commercial data/AI is a named function worth building out in public, or the company doesn't have the seat at all yet.
> 
> **By company type** — worth flagging as a tension in what I was asked to do: the original brief told me to exclude agencies and vendors (CROs, staffing firms, consultancies) from scope, and I did — one agency posting (Barrington James, a staffing firm) surfaced and was correctly excluded. So this axis produced a single data point: **every posting in this report is at a manufacturer, by design.** I can't give you a real manufacturer-vs-agency-vs-vendor comparison without re-running the search with agencies and vendors deliberately included, which the original scope told me not to do. Flagging rather than quietly picking one instruction over the other.
> 
> **By brand or therapeutic area named:** roughly 9 of the 33 full-live postings name a specific brand or therapeutic area — AstraZeneca's PNH-specific director (snippet only, not in the 33), GSK's Oncology and Vaccines-specific data science directors (snippet), AbbVie's Oncology and Parkinson's-specific roles (closed), Takeda's GI Franchise and Oncology roles, Regeneron's Neurology-specific associate director, BioNTech's Oncology-specific market research role, Exelixis's GI Franchise executive director (snippet, blocked). The large majority — roughly three-quarters — are portfolio-wide or enterprise-wide, not tied to one drug or disease area.

> <result># Skeptic Review — Pharma Commercial Data/AI Job Market Research
> 
> I ran nine independent searches to test these claims rather than take the lane reports at face value. Findings below.
> 
> ## Claim-by-claim
> 
> **Claim 1 — Market vocabulary. WEAKENED, and possibly mis-scoped.**
> Direct search turned up "customer data" in job **titles** at two of the largest pharma companies in the industry: Sanofi's "Director, Customer Data Management Lead" (owns US customer data MDM strategy) and Johnson &amp; Johnson's "Global Customer Data Platform Lead." Leo Pharma has "Director, Commercial Data Management." This directly contradicts "customer data almost never appears." Separately, the claim as written is scoped to "agency and vendor postings" — but the sample-gap disclosure says boutique agencies were never researched. If that's true, Claim 1's core assertion may describe zero actual agency data. Either the claim's scope was silently widened in the writeup (from agencies to the whole market), or it was never tested against the population it names. On the positive side, "claims data," "real-world data/evidence," and "Next Best Action/Engagement" are genuinely common terms of art — I found live Sanofi and J&amp;J postings using "Next Best Engagement" and "Next Best Action" verbatim, and RWD/RWE director roles are widespread (Jazz, Formation Bio, IQVIA). So the vocabulary-shift observation isn't fabricated — but "customer data almost never appears" is falsified at the title level, and the agency-specific framing looks unsourced.
> 
> **Claim 2 — One-seat-four-jobs is rare. WEAKENED (directionally plausible, coding validity untested).**
> Two lanes converging on similarly low rates (2/39, 1/20) is reassuring, not damning. But "explicit language for all four" is a coding choice, not a fact, and no inter-rater check is reported — no double-coding, no disagreement rate. Postings routinely imply stacking through fragments ("owns P&amp;L," "leads external partnerships," "manages team of 12") without ever stating "strategy + delivery + people + BD" in one sentence. A stricter bar mechanically produces a lower count; that's not evidence the norm doesn't exist, it's evidence the instrument is conservative. The direction (stacking is the exception) is probably real; the magnitude is not established.
> 
> **Claim 3 — Zero C-suite, AD at 36%. SPLIT: the observation SURVIVES, the interpretation is KILLED.**
> It's well-established recruiting practice that C-suite roles go through retained search and are rarely posted publicly — this is not a discovery, it's how executive hiring works everywhere, not just pharma AI. So "zero C-suite postings" is very likely an accurate fact about job boards. But treating that as evidence about where organizations invest is a category error the claim itself flags and should have stopped there. Report the fact; kill the inference.
> 
> **Claim 4 — Outcome specificity is higher than expected. WEAKENED — likely comparing different constructs.**
> "Names a concrete decision, metric, or workflow" bundles three different things. A posting that says "uses claims data to build HCP targeting models" names a workflow and a data source but not necessarily the decision the AI serves (which channel, which patient segment, which budget gets reallocated). The prior 347-posting baseline (15%) was reportedly measuring "which decision AI would operationalize" specifically — a narrower bar. If the fresh lanes coded "mentions something specific" as a hit, the jump from 15% to ~60% (24/39) or ~60% (12/20) is not a real trend, it's two different rulers. This needs the operational definitions checked before it's reported as a finding at all, let alone as evidence bearing on the thesis.
> 
> **Claim 5 — Small-cap is all-or-nothing. WEAKENED to KILLED.**
> 7 of 8 small-cap postings from one company is n=1 at the company level. My own search surfaced other small/mid biotech data leadership postings (VP Head of Data Science &amp; Biostatistics roles, director-level analytics roles at companies outside the lane's sample), which at minimum contradicts a clean binary. A category-level claim ("small companies either build a named function or have none") cannot stand on one company's hiring calendar. This reads as an anecdote wearing a segment-level label.
> 
> **Claim 6 — Consulting demand is invisible on job boards. WEAKENED — unconfirmed, not disproven.**
> I found real evidence that pharma AI/operating-model assessment work exists as a sold service (Deloitte, Accenture, and boutique AI-consulting firms all market "90-day diagnostic" / data-maturity-audit offerings), consistent with "sold, not posted." But I could not confirm or rule out whether this work surfaces on procurement portals, RFP aggregators, or government/public-sector tenders (e.g., SAM.gov, NHS/HHS-adjacent tenders) — I didn't get a clean hit either way, and nothing suggests Lane C checked those channels either. Six live contract postings is a thin base for a "generally true" claim about an entire market segment. Report this as a plausible, unverified hypothesis — not a finding.
> 
> **Claim 7 — India GCCs are where senior data/AI hiring is moving. SURVIVES.**
> This is the best-supported claim in the set. Independent sources beyond the lane's three companies corroborate the same direction: Novartis Hyderabad described as "the benchmark pharma GCC for C-suite executive search" (8,000 employees, 20% of global headcount); AstraZeneca's Chennai center leading global AI drug discovery and data science; GSK's Bengaluru/Hyderabad centers as a "consistent generator of demand for senior technology and commercial leadership"; Sanofi's GCC expansion described as "one of the largest senior leadership hiring pipelines in pharma over the next 18 months." Four to five companies, multiple independent sources, consistent mechanism (global function ownership, not just execution, moving to India). This one holds up.
> 
> ## Sample-integrity attacks
> 
> - **Stale-but-indexed postings (~1/3):** This doesn't just add noise — it likely biases toward senior/complex roles, which take longer to fill and stay listed-but-dead longer than junior reqs. That inflates apparent seniority concentration (feeds Claim 3's AD-36% number) and inflates apparent role complexity (feeds Claim 4). Any claim about *current* market intensity is unsupported until dead listings are stripped.
> - **Six large pharma blocked, nine small/mid-caps never touched, boutique agencies never researched:** This is fatal to Claim 5 (small-cap generalization drawn while 9 small-caps were never looked at) and to Claim 1's agency framing (the agencies the claim is about were never sampled). It also means the six blocked large-pharma sites — likely the companies with the most mature, most defended career infrastructure — are systematically absent, which could easily flip the seniority and vocabulary findings if their listings look different (they often do: more formalized title ladders, more legal-reviewed language).
> - **Indexability bias:** Job boards favor companies using standard ATS platforms with public APIs (Workday, Greenhouse feeds to LinkedIn/Indeed). Companies with custom or gated career sites — often the largest, most bureaucratic organizations — are underrepresented. That skews the whole sample toward mid-size, aggregator-friendly employers, which plausibly also skews toward more standardized, less bespoke language — which could itself be *producing* some of the vocabulary convergence Claims 1 reports, rather than reflecting an industry-wide linguistic shift.
> 
> ## The thesis question
> 
> The fresh 2026 evidence **does not test the thesis** — it can't. The thesis is that organizations fail at AI because they skip operating-model design (undefined decision rights, undefined accountability), not because of a real talent shortage. None of the seven claims measure operating-model definition directly. The closest proxies — low outcome-specificity (Claim 4) and low role-stacking (Claim 2) — are being read as "companies hire without defining the decision" and "roles are fragmented," but neither was designed to distinguish "the organization hasn't defined the operating model" from equally plausible alternatives: specialization is simply normal at scale, or postings are just badly written by HR regardless of what the org has actually defined internally. A job posting's specificity is evidence about the posting, not directly about the organization's internal governance.
> 
> There's a second-order problem worth naming directly: the fresh findings — fragmented seniority, absent C-suite ownership, low decision-specificity, single-company-driven small-cap chaos — all happen to point in the direction the thesis would predict. Given that the coder plausibly knew the thesis while doing subjective coding (what counts as "explicit," what counts as "names the decision"), this alignment is exactly the pattern confirmation bias produces. That doesn't mean the thesis is wrong. It means this research cannot be used to say it's right, because it wasn't built to be capable of proving it wrong.
> 
> ## Three findings to trust
> 1. **India GCCs are absorbing senior data/AI leadership, not just execution** (Claim 7) — externally corroborated by multiple independent sources across 4-5 companies.
> 2. **C-suite AI/data roles are essentially invisible on job boards** (Claim 3, narrowly stated) — consistent with how executive search works generally; report as a fact about job boards, never as a fact about organizational investment.
> 3. **Explicit four-way role stacking (strategy + delivery + people + BD) is rare, not the norm** (Claim 2, directionally) — two independent lanes converged on the same low range even with an admittedly strict bar.
> 
> ## Three findings not to report at all
> 1. **"Customer data" almost never appears** (Claim 1) — directly falsified by live Sanofi and J&amp;J job titles; the claim's own stated scope (agency/vendor postings) appears never to have been actually sampled.
> 2. **Outcome specificity jumped from 15% to ~60%** (Claim 4) — likely comparing "mentions something specific" against a stricter prior definition of "names the operationalized decision." Not a trend; a metric mismatch.
> 3. **Small-cap is all-or-nothing** (Claim 5) — one company producing 88% of the small-cap sample is not a market pattern.
> 
> ## The single most important thing this research failed to establish
> It never measured the actual construct the thesis is about — whether organizations have defined the operating model (decision rights, accountability, what the role is *for*) before they hire. Every claim here is a proxy (vocabulary, title, seniority, posting behavior), and none of the proxies were validated against the construct they're being used to stand in for. The research can describe what the job market looks like. It cannot currently say why organizations fail at AI, and reporting it as if it does — especially where the findings conveniently confirm the prior 2025 thesis — would be presenting decoration as confirmation.
>

Merged and saved at [job-market-scan--MERGE--2026-08-13.md](reference/job-market-scan--MERGE--2026-08-13.md).

## The correction

- **I told you "customer data almost never appears." That was wrong.**
- Sanofi has a live "Director, Customer Data Management Lead." J&J has a "Global Customer Data Platform Lead." Leo Pharma has "Director, Commercial Data Management."
- The claim was also about agency postings, and **no boutique agencies were ever sampled.** It described a population nobody studied.

## Two more findings killed

- **Outcome specificity did not rise from 15% to 60%.** Two different rulers. Your 2025 number measured whether a posting names the decision the AI serves. The fresh lanes counted any concrete mention, including a dataset name. A dataset is not a decision.
- **"Small-cap is all-or-nothing" is dead.** One company produced seven of the eight small-cap postings, and nine similar companies were never checked.

## What survived

- **India capability centres are absorbing senior data and AI leadership**, not just execution. Best-supported finding in the scan, corroborated outside the lanes.
- **Four-way role stacking is rare, not the norm.** Both lanes converged. That weakens your prior belief rather than confirming it.
- **The salary bands**, which are real and usable: senior director $224,000 to $348,000, VP up to $401,350, agency analytics director $130,000 to $180,000.
- **"Next Best Engagement," "Next Best Action," "agentic AI," "data enablement"** as live terms of art.

## The thing you actually asked for

- **The scan cannot test your thesis.** Nothing in it measures whether a company defined its operating model before hiring.
- **A vague job ad and an undefined operating model look identical from outside.** Badly written HR copy explains the data just as well.
- The skeptic's warning, which is the reason you wanted this unbiased: the findings all point the way your thesis predicts, and that alignment is exactly what confirmation bias produces. It doesn't make the thesis wrong. It makes this evidence unable to prove it right.

## What would test it

- **One question, asked to a real buyer: before you opened that role, had you decided what decision it would own?**
- That's a conversation, not a search. Which puts us back at people who'll take your call.

**One next action:** the salary bands and the terms of art are usable right now regardless of the thesis. They set your pricing floor and fix how the offer gets worded. That's the piece I'd take forward.

Then you have the answer the research couldn't get, and it counts — you were in the room. But there's a catch worth seeing before you build positioning on it.

## Your evidence is better than the postings

- **99 transcripts of being inside these organizations** while they failed at exactly this.
- The shadow system nobody trusted. "Why didn't we address that then?" "We're kind of flying blind."
- **That's the construct measured directly**, which no job posting can do.

## The catch

- **You only ever saw the companies that hired outside help.**
- Companies that defined the decision, built the operating model and made it work **never called you.** They had no reason to.
- So your sample is selected on failure. It's the emergency room, not the population.
- **You cannot say "organizations skip operating model design" from it.** You can only say the ones who called you had.

## Why that turns out not to matter

- **Your buyers are exactly that selected population.** The ones who call are the ones who failed.
- The claim doesn't need to be true of all pharma. **It needs to be true of the companies who will hire you**, and there you have direct evidence.
- That's a narrower claim and a stronger one, because it's the only version you can actually defend.

## How the wording changes

- **Weak, and unprovable:** organizations fail at AI because they skip operating model design.
- **Strong, and yours:** every time I've been called in, nobody had decided what decision the system was supposed to serve. That was true before AI and it's worse with it.
- The second one is a story from inside the room. The first is a claim someone can argue with.

## Where this leaves the thesis

- **Keep it. Stop trying to prove it with market data.**
- It's a practitioner's observation with ten years behind it, not a research finding, and it's more persuasive that way.
- **The postings were never going to validate it**, and now we know why rather than guessing.

**One next action:** that reframe is the first line of your offer. "By the time someone calls me, nobody has decided what decision the system was supposed to serve." Everything else — the assessment, the price, the site — hangs off that sentence.

That inverts my selection-bias point, and in your favor. I had it backwards: you weren't seeing the failures, you were seeing the ones thinking ahead, and they still didn't have it.

## The distinction you just made

- **"Skip" implies they considered it and passed.** That's the word my analysis used and it's wrong.
- **"Build around it, not realizing they need it"** is a different problem entirely.
- Skipping is a decision. **Building around a gap you can't see is a blind spot.**
- You cannot sell a fix for a problem nobody knows they have. You have to make it visible first.

## The finding hiding in what you said

- **You have never heard anyone say "analytic operating model" or "data operating model."** Not once, across many agencies and brands, over years.
- That's not a small observation. **A thing with no name in a market has no budget line, no owner, and no vendor category.**
- It also explains why every fix gets pointed at tools and hires instead. Those have names.

## Why this is stronger evidence than I credited

- If the companies who called you were the ones **already thinking ahead**, and even they were "nowhere near," the population claim gets stronger, not weaker.
- One or two out of a hundred, and those two only on the surface.
- **The best-prepared cases still failing is harder evidence than the worst cases failing.**

## What it does to the offer

- **You are not selling a solution to a stated problem.** You're selling the moment someone sees the problem.
- That's exactly what a diagnostic is for, and it's why the assessment shape fits rather than a build.
- **It also means you cannot lead with the term.** Nobody is searching for an operating model assessment. They'd have to already know.
- You lead with what they do feel: they can't see what they actually have, and they don't trust it.

## The naming problem, and the opportunity in it

- **An unnamed problem can't be bought.** It can also be named by whoever names it first.
- That's the strongest content position you have: you've watched a hundred companies build around a thing none of them had a word for.
- **You do not need to invent a clever label.** You need to describe the gap in the words they already use, then say what it's called.

**One next action:** this is the piece of positioning that has been missing all day, and it came from you in one message. Say it out loud once more, plainly, as if to a data leader who's never met you: what is the thing they built around, and how would they know they did it? That answer is the offer's first paragraph.

## The claim every specialist makes

## The question that would settle it

## The harder problem, which scarcity doesn't solve

- **Rarity only converts to revenue if the buyer can tell the difference.**
- There are hundreds of people whose landing pages say exactly what you'd say. From outside, you look like them.
- **The buyer has no way to distinguish someone who has done it from someone who read about it**, unless you hand them one.
- That's what dated artifacts do. Work from 2013, 2014, 2019, 2021 is the one thing nobody can fabricate.

## So the positioning has two jobs, not one

- **Make the gap visible**, since they built around it without a name for it.
- **Make yourself checkable**, since the claim itself is crowded.
- The first is content. The second is proof, and it's the piece you've had all along and never shown.

Running against the transcripts now. The bar is defined before scoring, so it can't be moved to fit the answer.

## What it's testing

- **Did anyone else originate a connection across three or more layers** — the data structure, the workflow using it, the decision it serves, what breaks if it's wrong, who owns it.
- Deep expertise in one layer doesn't count. Neither does agreeing with someone else's systems argument.
- **Your own turns get quoted as the baseline**, so the comparison is visible rather than assumed.

## The counter-explanation it has to rule out

- **You were often hired to be the one thinking that way.** If you were cast as the strategist, of course you strategised.
- So it's looking for moments where a client-side person **had the opening and didn't take it**, versus moments where nobody had the floor.
- That difference decides whether this is about capability or about casting. **They point to very different positioning.**

## It's also looking for the opposite

- Places where a specialist caught something you missed, or corrected you on substance.
- **If none exist across 99 meetings, that's suspicious**, not flattering.

If it comes back that two or three others cleared the bar, that's still a good outcome. It means you're in a small field rather than alone, and small fields are easier to sell into than empty ones.

> **5. The buyer's problem.** A pharma data leader searching for this help today would find generic consulting-firm service pages, one boutique with a relevant-sounding name but no data-specific proof, and one independent consultant with real-looking but anonymized numbers. There's no clear signal a buyer could use to separate real track record from marketing — which is itself informative: it suggests the category is too new and too small for a reputation market to have formed yet.
> 
> **Verdict on Part 2:** The scarcity claim points **true, but not for a dramatic reason** — it isn't that the skill is rare in some special sense; it's that the specific *combination* (data operating model design + pharma marketing context, named and provable) is a narrow intersection that the market hasn't organized around yet. Supply exists at the generalist-consultancy layer (ZS, PwC can do it as part of broader engagements) and at the boutique/individual layer it's genuinely thin — one clearly-positioned boutique, one clearly-positioned individual, no visible competitive set beneath the big firms. This is closer to "thin because nobody's built the category yet" than "thin because it's an elite skill" — but the search cannot fully distinguish those two explanations, and every specialist has an interest in believing the latter, so this should be read as directional, not conclusive.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## PART 3: Do companies claim the four capabilities, and does anyone show proof?
> 
> The four claims tested: (1) consistent, repeatable reporting, (2) data analytics that actually gets used, (3) a singular customer view, (4) omnichannel at the right time/place.
> 
> **Who claims them:** Extremely common. Nearly every vendor, agency, and consultancy page surfaced in this entire research pass makes some version of these four claims — "unified customer profiles," "single source of truth," "right message, right time, right channel," "consistent reporting across teams." This language is close to universal in pharma marketing/analytics marketing copy (Improvado, Viseven, PulsePoint, indigitall, Anthill, and dozens of similar vendor blogs all use nearly interchangeable phrasing).
> 
> **Who shows anything resembling proof, and the strongest example found:**
> - **Sanofi / G&amp;CO case study** (g-co.agency) — the strongest numbers found: cut "data activation latency from three days to under three hours," delivered "30% lift in commercial conversion across more than 18 global markets," via a centralized Digital Accelerator building real-time "golden profiles." This is the single most specific, most quantified claim in the entire search. **But it is vendor-authored marketing** (G&amp;CO, an agency, publishing about its own client work) — exactly the trap flagged: the vendor chose which numbers to show, and Sanofi presumably approved the case study. It cannot be weighted as independent proof, only as the best-dressed example of a claim.
> - **OptimizeRx chemotherapy case study** — 10.5% script lift, 7.4:1 ROI — same category: vendor case study, real numbers, unverifiable methodology, client-approved.
> - **Robert Izquierdo's anonymized metrics** (60% reporting-lag reduction, etc.) — same pattern, self-disclosed and explicitly anonymized.
> 
> **Practitioner accounts that push back — the more credible evidence, per the instruction to weight these higher:**
> - **Amaninder Dhillon, PharmaState Academy, "Single Customer View (SCV) — Pharma Oblivion of 360-Degree Customer Dashboard"** (Nov 2022) — direct critique: *"not many Pharma companies have adopted, integrated, or leveraged [available tools] to their full potential,"* and that customer insight is often *"used as a secret weapon to impress hierarchy and kill internal competitors"* rather than genuinely shared/operationalized.
> - **msg industry advisors, "Beyond the Buzz"** (~Jan 2023, consultancy but candid) — *"results often fall short of expectations. Instead of achieving improvements, companies face increased complexity"* and *"few companies have succeeded in effectively implementing these strategies."*
> - **A synthesized practitioner pattern surfaced repeatedly across searches** (independent of any single source): companies "spent millions on data integration platforms without changing incentives or KPIs, resulting in integrated data that nobody used because individual functions still relied on their own dashboards showing metrics they were rewarded for" — and a specific, checkable technical symptom: analysts "repeatedly asking 'are these the same customer?'" because no customer master ID was established before ingestion.
> - **Andrea Langella**, an identifiable independent life-sciences marketing consultant (MSc molecular biology, decade of pharma product/measurement experience, designed measurement frameworks across 12 markets) — writes specifically on "The Omnichannel Measurement Problem in Pharma," a practitioner voice naming the gap directly (full page blocked on fetch, but positioning and title confirmed independently).
> - **Fierce Pharma Week 2025 conference session** (Sept 10, 2025), presented by Lauren Jones, Senior Director of Digital Operations, Strategy and Analytics at **Incyte** — session titled *"Is Omnichannel a Flop in Pharma?"* — a named practitioner at a real pharma company, on a real conference stage, framing the question exactly as skeptically as the practitioner behind this research did. This is the closest thing found to an insider saying, on the record, that the claim may not match the reality.
> 
> **The ratio:** Overwhelmingly claim-heavy. Every vendor/agency page claims all four capabilities; maybe one in fifteen-to-twenty sources encountered offered anything closer to proof, and even the "proof" sources split into two camps — vendor case studies with real-sounding numbers and unverifiable methodology (Sanofi/G&amp;CO, OptimizeRx), versus practitioner accounts that contain no flattering numbers at all but instead name specific mechanical failure modes (no customer master ID, misaligned incentives, dashboards nobody trusts). If the standard is "named metrics + methodology detailed enough to check + third-party validation," essentially **nothing in this search cleared that bar** — even the Sanofi case study fails it, because "golden profiles" and "30% lift" are asserted, not shown.
> 
> **Is "single customer view" / "right time right place" pure marketing language now?** Yes, functionally. Both phrases appear in nearly identical form across dozens of unrelated vendor pages with no differentiation in what they actually mean operationally — a strong sign they've become table-stakes marketing copy rather than a signal of real capability. The PharmaState Academy piece makes this explicit, dubbing it "Pharma Oblivion."
> 
> **Verdict on Part 3:** This is a market where **everyone claims and almost nobody proves** — and importantly, the practitioners who write candidly (Dhillon, msg-advisors, the Incyte conference session, the recurring "integrated data nobody used" pattern) are the ones saying so directly, unprompted, years apart (2022–2025), which is stronger evidence than any single vendor case study either way. The one genuinely strong-looking proof point (Sanofi/G&amp;CO) is disqualified by the vendor-marketing trap the brief specifically warned about. Per the caveat in the brief: absence of public proof is not proof of absence — some pharma companies may have real, working single-customer-view infrastructure they simply don't publicize. But nothing surfaced in this search demonstrates that; what surfaced is claim on one side and skeptical practitioner testimony on the other.
>

**Claude** · `79710a46-f719-4ff7-a911-9a4a9420c5e1`

Your hedge was right, almost exactly. Here's what came back.

## "Changed a bit, not much" — confirmed, and precisely

- **The term is real, thin, and recent.** Every credible hit is 2025 or 2026.
- **It lives in two places:** large consultancy sales content, and enterprise data-management job titles. Moderna has a live director role for "designing and advancing the global operating model."
- **It is not in the room you were in.** Zero of four big healthcare agencies use the language about themselves. Zero of eight boutique pharma analytics firms name it as a service.
- So it's entering at the data and IT layer, not the marketing layer. **Your observation holds exactly where you made it.**
- The most common adjacent phrase is "data governance model," which is a narrower thing.

## The field is thin, and one name matters

- A buyer searching for this today finds **two big generalists where it's one line item, one boutique selling it generically, and one individual.**
- **That individual is Robert Izquierdo**, positioning around "the marketing data model and operating rules." He shows numbers and flags them as anonymized and not verifiable.
- **That's your competitive set.** Not hundreds. One clearly positioned person and some enterprise firms.

## But not for the reason you'd want

- The honest read: **thin because nobody has built the category, not because the skill is elite.**
- Every specialist believes the second one. The evidence supports the first.
- **That's better news.** An unbuilt category rewards whoever names it. A credentials war rewards whoever has the biggest logo.

## Your four-question test, validated

- **Everyone claims all four. Almost nobody proves any.**
- Roughly one source in fifteen to twenty offers anything like proof, and **nothing cleared the bar** of named metrics plus checkable method.
- The best-looking proof was a vendor writing about its own client work. Real numbers, unverifiable, client-approved. Disqualified.
- **"Single customer view" and "right time, right place" are now table-stakes marketing copy**, used identically across dozens of unrelated vendors.

## Three insiders said your thing out loud, years apart

- A practitioner in 2022: pharma's "oblivion of the 360-degree customer dashboard," and insight used "as a secret weapon to impress hierarchy" rather than shared.
- An advisory in 2023: "few companies have succeeded in effectively implementing these strategies."
- **September 2025, on a Fierce Pharma Week stage, a senior director at Incyte gave a session titled "Is Omnichannel a Flop in Pharma?"**
- That last one is a named person at a real pharma company asking your question in public. **You are not alone in the read, and you are early to saying it plainly.**

## What this settles

- **The gap is real and the words for it barely exist.** That's the content position.
- **The proof gap is the offer.** Everyone claims four things, nobody substantiates them, and you can check all four in two weeks.
- **The competitive set is nearly empty**, which means the risk isn't losing to someone better. It's nobody knowing the category exists.

**One next action:** that Incyte session title is a gift. "Is omnichannel a flop in pharma" is your post two, written from inside the room rather than from a stage, and it points straight at the assessment.

First transcript is back, and it goes against you. Delivering it straight.

## The hypothesis fails in this meeting

- **One other person cleared the bar six times.** The report ranks his schema-dependency argument as stronger than anything you said in that meeting.
- **A second person cleared it twice**, with a maintenance-debt argument nobody else made.
- **You were corrected on substance three times, and conceded each time.**

## What he caught that you missed

- **On prescription data:** you assumed it should be treated like engagement data. He pointed out it carries no campaign and doesn't need the same isolation. Your reply: "I'm relying on your expertise to make that difference."
- **On the segment builder demo:** you showed a Google Analytics filter as a stand-in. He said it isn't the same thing, and explained why. You said "I know it's not the same."
- **On "it's already existing":** you said that repeatedly about the build. He came back with the team having no Clojure expertise, no documented proof it was doable, and a timeline he called a nightmare.

## His strongest moment, which outranks yours in that file

> "I'm gonna make an assumption that the data will come in a form that is consumable. But if it doesn't, then we have a blame on Audienceology, which we can't. So Audienceology should tell us the schema."

That connects a data structure, a workflow, a downstream failure, and who carries the blame. Four of five layers in one breath.

## Two caveats that are real, not consolation

- **This is one meeting out of 99**, and it's an internal build meeting. Technical leads shine there by design. The other 98 are still being read.
- **It's unclear who he works for.** He's described as owning the delivery process and speaking of "our developers." If he's the delivery vendor rather than the client, then the client-side people still weren't doing this, and the finding changes shape considerably.

## What I'd take from it either way

- **"I was the only one" is not going to survive.** Something narrower will.
- The version that might hold: **the person who could see it was rarely the person being asked**, and rarely on the client's side of the table.
- **That's still a sellable position**, and it's honest. Being one of a few beats being alone, because a market of one is not a market.

**One next action:** let the other 98 finish, then we'll know whether that person was the exception or the rule. If two or three names come back repeatedly, we position against a small field rather than against silence.
